extracted.intended_audience: administrative analysts; public administration officials; government managers; business procedure analysts
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria for analyzing, designing, and improving administrative procedure in large organizations, covering organization, planning, execution, control, purchasing, personnel, measurement, scheduling, and related methods. Written as a practical handbook for the administrative analyst.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phases of administration
rubrics_metrics.description: planning — deciding what is to be done; execution — giving orders, instructions, and supervision; and control — seeing that the work is actually done according to plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three phases as the basic analytic frame: each administrative task involves planning, execution, and control; coordination extends into all three phases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good procedure (circulation of business)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good procedure is that which allows business to circulate smoothly and rapidly, and with the fewest interruptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate procedures by how well they promote 'good circulation' (minimal lost motion, few stoppages). Stoppages at any point can paralyze other parts of the organization; focus on flow and removal of bottlenecks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative organization: clarity of relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Administration requires organization so that each individual has one supervisor (or occasionally more) from whom he receives orders and to whom he is responsible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether employees know where they stand, what they have to do, and who their boss is; unclear or hazy organizational arrangements often require outside investigation to unravel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegation and cumulative responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrators must delegate much work to subordinates; the reverse side is cumulative responsibility making each individual answerable for subordinates' work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that delegation is appropriate, responsibilities are cumulative and understood, and that arrangements (e.g., functional foremanship) do not leave employees with multiple conflicting bosses unless authority to overrule is clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scalar (hierarchical) organization and its modifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Scalar (hierarchical) organization is the basic form; specialization requires modification into organization by purpose, process, or area of operation, or combinations thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify what mix (purpose/process/area) the organization actually uses and whether that structure suits the tasks being performed; beware of mismatch between drawn charts and actual operating structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between purpose and process (program vs procedure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fundamental distinction between the purpose (what you administer) and the process (how you administer it)—between program and procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative analysis must consider both direct activities (programs) and the business of managing them (procedure/administrative management); improvements may be needed in either domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific approach to administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Study administration in an exact and, so far as possible, scientific way: stick closely to observed facts and be systematic in analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use social-science concepts grounded in reality; avoid abstract theorizing disconnected from observed office phenomena; treat procedure as a pattern of human behavior requiring both measurement and qualitative observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance freedom and regimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Administration must encourage creative ability and initiative yet coordinate the work of hundreds of people; this conflict between individual freedom and social need for regimentation is central.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design procedures that avoid oppressive rules while ensuring necessary coordination; evaluate rules for whether they suppress initiative unnecessarily or fail to coordinate effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of procedural rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules of administrative procedure arise from customs, specific official orders, statutes, and other sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating procedure, identify rule origins (custom, statute, order) and examine whether rules remain appropriate or are merely ritual remnants of past needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis by function, unit, and administrative sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative analysis can be done by function, by units of organization, or by administrative sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply all three analytical lenses as appropriate: function-analysis (what tasks), unit-analysis (who does them), sequence-analysis (flow of work). Cross-analysis charts and other tools help integrate perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of graphic methods (flow charts, cross-analysis charts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Graphic methods (flow charts, unit-production charts, cross-analysis charts) are essential tools for depicting organization, sequence, and distribution of work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare flow charts of paper and people movement; use cross-analysis charts to relate functions, units, and sequences; graphic displays expose bottlenecks, duplications, and unnecessary motions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement techniques for workload, timing, and scheduling
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques for gathering data on work load, timing, and scheduling (unit production charts, timing studies, work-load measurement) are essential for scientific administrative analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure where feasible; recognize limits (creative discretionary work may not be tape-measurable); use measurement to set operating standards, detect backlogs, and schedule resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work distribution (assignment of tasks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Work distribution requires clear assignment of tasks and duties so that tasks are apportioned reasonably among units and individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze tasks to achieve balanced workloads, eliminate unnecessary duplication, and ensure tasks are grouped for efficiency; consider functional specialization versus generalist approaches depending on context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and scheduling of administrative work
rubrics_metrics.description: Timing of administrative work (when tasks occur, delay points) and scheduling (sequencing and timing of operations) are central to smooth operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess if scheduling minimizes idle time and congestion; use timing data to set realistic schedules and to assign staff so that peak loads are met and bottlenecks avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative control — need for planned control
rubrics_metrics.description: Control requires planned systems and devices to see that work is done as intended; administrative control includes concepts, patterns, devices, and diminishing returns considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate existence and effectiveness of control devices (reports, inspections, audits, operating standards), how control relationships are designed (span, review points), and whether controls produce diminishing returns or stifle initiative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management planning vs administrative (program) planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate administrative (program) planning—deciding what shall be done—from management planning—determining how it shall be done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure both program planning and management planning are present: program planning sets objectives and scopes; management planning organizes resources, sequences work, and implements control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operating standards and measurement as control
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish and use operating standards and measurements (work-load standards, production charts) as part of control and production management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set realistic operating standards from measured data; use standards to plan staffing and identify inefficiencies; avoid arbitrary or oppressive quotas that ignore job variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination of unnecessary tasks and functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and eliminate unnecessary tasks and functions as a means of increasing administrative efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use task analysis and measurements to find redundant or obsolete routines; beware of ritualized procedures preserved by custom without current purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of correspondence and channels of contact
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures should define channels of contact and classification of correspondence so papers are routed to the proper persons and do not cause confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map routing rules (e.g., which papers go to A,B,K for initialing then to M for signature); assess 'clearance' and routing practices; reduce unnecessary circulation and redundant handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line and staff distinction and staff authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear demarcation between line functions and staff functions; staff officers' authority and appropriate uses must be defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether staff and line roles are properly assigned, whether staff officers have appropriate advisory versus directive authority, and whether staff arrangements avoid confusion and conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committees: purpose, composition, and use
rubrics_metrics.description: Committees are a recurring administrative device; their use must be evaluated for necessity, composition, and effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess committee functions (planning, coordination, review), minimize redundant committees, ensure clear charges, membership, and decision procedures to avoid wasted time and diffusion of responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralization vs decentralization
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions on centralization and devolution must balance control needs and efficiency; centralization affects coordination, morale, and responsiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze where central control is necessary (policy, budgets) and where decentralization increases efficiency; consider span of control, inspection burdens, and diminishing returns of over-centralization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purchasing and procurement procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Purchasing procedures include open-market purchases, bids, term contracts, consolidation of federal purchases, and bid handling rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine procurement methods for economy, technical standardization, inspection provisions, and avoidance of pyramiding or inefficient buying; consider central procurement vs decentralized purchasing in context of volume and technical control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personnel procedures: appointment, civil service, classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Personnel administration includes appointment procedures, civil service examinations, classification of positions, reserve/exchange services, and emergency agency staffing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether civil service procedures, classification, and appointment mechanisms supply needed staff, maintain morale, and permit flexibility (e.g., reserve forces) while ensuring fairness and competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure manuals and promulgation
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure should be codified in manuals and promulgated so employees know standardized methods and responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review availability, clarity, and currency of procedure manuals; ensure manuals are practical, used, and accompanied by training rather than merely ritual documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspection and integrating inspection as control
rubrics_metrics.description: Inspection (integrating inspection) serves as a control device to ensure adherence to procedure and identify problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess inspection policies: frequency, criteria, confidentiality, reporting lines; use inspection to detect operational deviations and recommend corrective actions without creating oppressive oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operating reports and production control
rubrics_metrics.description: Operating reports provide the data for management control and production planning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design concise, relevant operating reports that feed timely control actions; avoid excessive reporting that creates paperwork burdens without managerial use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical standardization and control
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical standardization (specifications, consolidated standards) is an important technique to control procurement, quality, and repetitive operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement technical standards where feasible to reduce inspection and purchasing complexity; ensure standards are periodically reviewed to match technical progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordination to avoid cross-purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Coordination is required so individuals and units do not work at cross-purposes; it extends into planning, execution, and control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate coordination mechanisms (channels of contact, regular conferences, committees, staff functions) and their effectiveness at preventing duplicated effort and conflicting actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of formalism and ritual in procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures may be dictated by habit and ritual rather than present needs; formalism can impede efficient administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and remove ritualized practices preserved from past needs; ensure procedures serve current organizational goals rather than tradition for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytical tools: cross-analysis, unit-production, flow charts
rubrics_metrics.description: Use analytical tools—cross-analysis charts, unit-production charts, flow charts, graphic methods—to reveal causes and effects in procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these tools to correlates of work (functions, units, sequences) to derive principles for planning efficient procedure and to visualize bottlenecks, workloads, and flows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human, socio-psychological factors and morale
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative technique must account for human and psychological elements; morale, employee relations, and the physical environment affect administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess physical conditions, morale impacts of controls or schedules, employee relations policies; avoid designs that harm morale even if mechanically efficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Span of control and diminishing returns
rubrics_metrics.description: Span of control matters; there are diminishing returns to expanding span beyond the point where supervision and coordination break down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze appropriate supervisory spans in context (complexity of work, need for coordination); watch for over- or under-supervision and adjust organization accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification and management of bottlenecks and backlogs
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative 'bottlenecks' and backlogs impede flow and must be detected and remedied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use flow analysis and measurement to locate bottlenecks, redistribute work, add capacity or change sequence to eliminate backlogs; consider both temporary and systemic causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work units and unit production measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Define work units and measure unit production to enable scheduling and workload balancing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish manageable unit measures where possible; use unit-production charts to show output over time and to plan staffing and timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data requirements for planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Planning requires adequate data (operations data, workload measures, timing, standards) to be realistic and usable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect necessary data before setting plans; use measurement and reports to feed planning and to revise plans as conditions change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promulgation and specification of administrative tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural divisions and specification of administrative tasks must be located and promulgated—management planning units and procedure divisions should be clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure roles for procedure planning are assigned (procedure divisions, planning units), that promulgation mechanisms exist, and that employees are trained in new procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to environment of administration (physical and political)
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical environment and political/legislative context affect administration and must be considered in procedural design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for work environment, legislative constraints, congressional oversight, and external political factors when designing procedures and controls.
